title: Galactic Rainbow
caption: The Milky Way over Gemini South, Cerro Pachón
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab/AURA/Kwon o chul

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The colourful band of the Milky Way stretches above the 8.1-meter Gemini South telescope, its bright star fields crossed by winding dust lanes. The Galactic Center sits directly above the telescope, and the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds appear on the left side of the picture.

The Magellanic Clouds are dwarf irregular galaxies that orbit the Milky Way as satellites. They lack the obvious spiral arms of larger neighbours such as the Andromeda Galaxy and are only a fraction of the Milky Way's size, but they still contain billions of stars. Together they are a prominent sight in southern night skies.

Gemini South stands on Cerro Pachón in the Chilean Andes. It is one of the two telescopes of the Gemini Observatory, and its twin, Gemini North, works from Maunakea in Hawai‘i. Observing conditions at both sites are superb, and between them the two telescopes can cover the entire night sky.

understand.summary: A panorama stitched from 10 images by astrophotographer Kwon o chul, each a 15-second exposure. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather more light than the eye can at a glance, so the colours and dust lanes probably stand out more than they would to someone on the mountain.

explore: When this photograph was released in 2019, the 8.4-meter Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) was soon due to arrive on Cerro Pachón beside Gemini South. It was designed to survey the whole visible sky every few nights. Astrophotographer Kwon o chul made the image for a planetarium time-lapse series, stitching together 10 frames of 15 seconds each into a panorama.
alt: The colourful band of the Milky Way above the Gemini South telescope, with the Magellanic Clouds on the left.
